opening_message: There's this tree in my yard with long feathery-looking leaves, and I keep noticing new little sprouts of it popping up nearby. Does anyone know what this actually is?

slots.name: leaf_rachis_wing
slots.value: The stem running down the middle of each leaf has these flat wing-like edges connecting the leaflets, kind of like a ridge.
slots.description: Presence of a winged rachis — a leaf-stem flange between leaflets unique to winged sumac (Rhus copallinum) among the region's compound-leaved trees/shrubs; tree-of-heaven never has this.

slots.name: leaflet_margins
slots.value: The little leaflets have tiny teeth or notches along the edges, not perfectly smooth.
slots.description: Leaflet margin texture — toothed/serrated leaflets point to sumac; tree-of-heaven's leaflets are smooth-edged.

slots.name: crushed_leaf_smell
slots.value: Doesn't smell like anything bad when a leaf gets crushed or torn.
slots.description: Absence of the strong rancid/burnt-peanut-butter odor tree-of-heaven releases when crushed — winged sumac has no such odor.

slots.name: bloom_appearance
slots.value: Back in summer it had these upright clusters of small greenish-yellow flowers standing up above the leaves, not hanging down.
slots.description: Flower cluster form/orientation — winged sumac's upright greenish-yellow clusters (July-Sept) differ from tree-of-heaven's cascading orange-to-brown clusters; an independent ID confirmation.

slots.name: new_shoots_location
slots.value: The new sprouts are coming up in a loose cluster around the base and a bit further out into the lawn, maybe ten stems total.
slots.description: Extent/pattern of resprouting — doesn't change the identification or the correct answer, since winged sumac's normal root-suckering habit is expected regardless of how many shoots are present.

slots.name: plant_height
slots.value: The main one is maybe 12 feet tall, multi-trunked, growing near the edge of the yard.
slots.description: Overall size — doesn't change the correct identification or framing regardless of height.

slots.name: fall_color
slots.value: Last fall the leaves turned a really bright red before dropping.
slots.description: Fall color is consistent with winged sumac but is a supportive, non-decisive cue on its own — not required to reach the correct identification.

slots.name: water_nearby
slots.value: There's a small drainage swale maybe 20 feet away that only has water in it after it rains.
slots.description: Water proximity — irrelevant here, since no herbicide treatment is warranted for this plant regardless of water presence.

ecological_framing_notes: Winged sumac is a native, non-invasive shrub with real wildlife value — it's an important winter food source for many birds, mammals, and pollinators including bees, and a larval host plant for the Luna moth and the Red-banded hairstreak butterfly. A correct answer should identify it as winged sumac (not tree-of-heaven), note that no herbicide or removal is needed, and ideally name this ecological value rather than just declining to treat it neutrally.
